content.text: FacebookLog InLog InForgot Account?Jason Simpson's PostJason Simpson Verified accountApril 1 at 10:51 PM · Shared with PublicLet’s talk about the incredible physics of what we’re seeing today! To get this crew to the Moon, we aren't just "going fast"—we're pushing the limits of atmospheric physics. Here is the speedometer breakdown for the Artemis II mission:𝙇𝙤𝙬 𝙀𝙖𝙧𝙩𝙝 𝙊𝙧𝙗𝙞𝙩 (~17,500 𝙢𝙥𝙝): This is the baseline. You have to hit 17.5k just to stay in orbit. Anything less and gravity wins, pulling you back into the atmosphere.𝙈𝙤𝙤𝙣𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙣𝙙 / 𝙏𝙧𝙖𝙣𝙨-𝙇𝙪𝙣𝙖𝙧 𝙄𝙣𝙟𝙚𝙘𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣 (~25,000 𝙢𝙥𝙝): This is the "Go" speed. After the upper stage finishes its burn, the crew will be screaming toward the Moon at roughly 25,000 mph.𝙏𝙝𝙚 "𝙀𝙨𝙘𝙖𝙥𝙚" 𝙁𝙖𝙘𝙩𝙤𝙧 (~25,020 𝙢𝙥𝙝): This is the exact mathematical point where you break Earth’s "gravitational rubber band" entirely. Since Artemis II is a "free-return" trajectory (meaning lunar gravity naturally slingshots them back home), they stay just a hair under this speed so they remain bound to the Earth-Moon system.𝙏𝙝𝙚 "𝙀𝙨𝙘𝙖𝙥𝙚" 𝙁𝙖𝙘𝙩𝙤𝙧 (~25,020 𝙢𝙥𝙝): When they come home in about 10 days, they’ll hit our atmosphere at this same speed. That’s about 7,500 mph faster than a Space Shuttle re-entry! That heat shield will be handling temperatures around 5,000°F—half as hot as the surface of the sun. Why such a specific speed? Think of Earth’s gravity like a deep "well." To climb out of it and reach the Moon, you have to generate enough kinetic energy to overcome that constant downward pull. At 25,020 mph (roughly 7 miles per second), your momentum finally matches the pull of gravity, allowing you to "escape" into deep space.All reactions:21868 comments37 sharesLikeCommentMost relevant Lucas JohnsonThe “free return trajectory” is one of the cooler parts of this as a built in safety feature. Once the burn happens to leave Earth orbit, the path will naturally loop around the moon and send us back to Earth. No engines required.
